strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of why softmax attention disperses and collapses representations in long contexts, and formally proves (with detailed appendix proofs) that α-entmax avoids these pathologies via non-vanishing attention, bounded entropy, representational preservation, and reduced gradient paths.

Introduces ASEntmax, a simple and practically appealing extension (per-head, per-query learnable log-power temperature scaling) that is compatible with fast sparse-attention kernels (AdaSplash) without architectural modification.
Proposes NAPE (NoPE+ALiBi hybrid), motivated by both theoretical analysis of positional-encoding interactions with sparse attention and empirical head-behavior studies (attention centroid analysis).

Extensive empirical validation across a diverse battery of synthetic length-generalization tasks (MQMTAR, Reverse, Copy, Sort, Max Retrieval, Flip-Flop, 2Back, Local Count) with many ablations (attention maps, gradient-norm/path measurements, learned β/γ distributions) that consistently support the theoretical claims.

Demonstrates striking extrapolation results (e.g., 1000x length generalization on associative recall, 76.7% accuracy at 65K tokens after training on 64 tokens), clearly outperforming softmax, Scalable-Softmax, and fixed-α entmax baselines.
Related work section and theoretical framing carefully position the contribution relative to recent work on softmax limitations, over-squashing, and positional encoding.
weaknesses: All controlled comparisons are performed on small synthetic tasks with very small models (2-10M parameters); the only language-modeling-scale experiment (120M params, FineWeb) is used solely to validate the functional form of learned scaling parameters, not to demonstrate downstream benefits of ASEntmax+NAPE on real text tasks, leaving the practical significance for actual LLMs unverified.

The Sort task fails to generalize beyond 4x for every method including ASEntmax, indicating the proposed approach does not uniformly solve length generalization and the paper could better characterize when/why it fails.

Theoretical guarantees are stated in terms of the support size s or sublinear growth exponent β, which are data/model-dependent quantities not directly controlled or predicted by the method; the practical translation from these asymptotic bounds to the observed empirical gains is not tightly established.

α is treated as a fixed hyperparameter (mostly α=1.5) throughout main experiments, with limited systematic study of how α interacts with the learned ASEntmax scaling parameters, despite the theory hinging heavily on α>1.
No efficiency/runtime comparison (e.g., against FlashAttention-based softmax at scale) is provided, despite motivating AdaSplash compatibility as a practical advantage.
Some experimental designs (e.g., choosing layer counts per baseline until softmax reaches a threshold generalization factor) could introduce comparison biases across methods.

The paper does not compare against other modern long-context approaches beyond softmax/SSMax/entmax variants (e.g., no comparison with state-space or hybrid attention architectures that are commonly used to address the same problem in practice).

strengths: The paper provides an extensive theoretical treatment of α-entmax properties (non-dispersion, representational preservation, over-squashing alleviation) with detailed proofs in the appendix, attempting to formally connect sparsity to known failure modes of softmax attention identified in prior work (Barbero et al. 2024; Veličković et al. 2024).

ASEntmax is a reasonably motivated extension that introduces head-specific, content- and length-aware temperature scaling, grounded in an argument from extreme-value theory for Gaussian logits (Remark 1).

The combination of NoPE and ALiBi heads (NAPE) is an interesting practical architectural idea, and the paper includes a reasonably thorough empirical study of how different attention transforms interact with different positional encoding schemes (NoPE, ALiBi, RoPE).

The experimental suite covers many synthetic tasks (MQMTAR, Copy, Reverse, Sort, Max Retrieval, Flip-Flop, 2Back, Local Count) with fairly careful ablations and many baselines (Softmax, SSMax, Adaptive Temperature, fixed-α entmax, ASEntmax, SEntmax, ASSMax), and reports some striking extrapolation numbers (e.g., 76.7% EM at 65K tokens after training at 64).
weaknesses: All empirical validation is restricted to small synthetic algorithmic tasks with tiny models (2-10M parameters); the only experiment approaching real language modeling scale (120M params, 5B tokens) is used solely to justify the functional form of the γ scaling curve-fit, not to evaluate actual downstream language modeling quality (perplexity, long-context QA, retrieval benchmarks, etc.), which severely undercuts the paper's central claim about 'long-context generalization' relevance to practical LLMs.

Several of the theoretical results (e.g., Lemma 1, Proposition 2/4's representational preservation counterexample) are existence proofs over specially constructed embeddings/logit configurations, not statements about what learned transformers actually do; this makes the practical relevance of these theorems to trained models unclear, and the gap between the constructed counterexamples and the empirical validation plots (which use similarly synthetic/controlled setups) is not well bridged.

Proposition 1's main concentration-resilience claim (part 3) explicitly assumes the attention support grows sublinearly as O(n^β); this is an assumption about learned behavior rather than something the paper shows transformers naturally achieve, so the entropy-boundedness claim is somewhat circular as stated.

The over-squashing analysis (Proposition 3/5) relies on strong simplifying assumptions (attention-value independence, constant-factor approximation of LayerNorm) carried over from Barbero et al. (2024), which the paper does not revisit or justify for the α-entmax setting, weakening the generality of the gradient-path argument.

No real efficiency/throughput/memory analysis is provided despite claims that scaling the query-key product 'allows direct use of fast optimized kernels... without modification' (AdaSplash); no wall-clock or memory comparison vs. softmax/FlashAttention is reported.

Results are reported as 'the single best-performing model selected from experiments conducted with multiple random seeds (3) and various learning rates' with no variance/error bars, which raises concerns about cherry-picking and reproducibility, especially given how sensitive synthetic length-generalization results are known to be to hyperparameters and seeds (cf. Zhou et al. 2024, Anil et al. 2022).

Several tasks show that the proposed method does not actually solve the stated problem (e.g., Sort fails beyond 4x for every method including ASEntmax; RoPE-based models fail almost universally beyond 2x regardless of attention mechanism), yet the abstract/conclusion broadly claim the method 'greatly outperforms' baselines and achieves 'robust long-context generalization,' which overstates what is empirically demonstrated.

No comparison against other structured/sparse attention mechanisms actually used in practice (Longformer, BigBird, sliding-window attention) or other recent length-generalization techniques beyond SSMax and Adaptive Temperature, despite these being discussed at length in Related Work.

The paper is extremely dense (40-page appendix with many propositions, proofs, and tables), which raises concerns about proper peer-reviewability and whether the core contributions (ASEntmax + NAPE) are sufficiently distilled and validated versus being padded with many loosely-connected theoretical results and ad hoc empirical analyses (e.g., choices like δ=1, specific ALiBi slopes 1/h) that lack sufficient justification or sensitivity analysis.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of why softmax attention disperses/collapses in long contexts and proves (with full derivations in the appendix) that α-entmax avoids these pathologies via non-vanishing attention, bounded entropy, representational preservation, and reduced gradient-path counts under over-squashing.

Introduces ASEntmax, a principled, head-specific learnable temperature scaling for entmax motivated by extreme-value theory of Gaussian logit ranges, and empirically shows it fits learned per-head scaling behavior in a real (if small-scale) language model better than prior scalar scaling approaches (SSMax).

Proposes NAPE (NoPE+ALiBi hybrid) and gives both theoretical analysis (interaction of α-entmax with NoPE/ALiBi/RoPE, hard attention windows, frequency-dependent cutoffs) and empirical attention-centroid visualizations that support the design choice.

Extensive synthetic-task evaluation suite (MQMTAR, Reverse, Copy, Sort, 2Back, Local Count, Flip-Flop, Max Retrieval) with systematic ablations across positional encodings (RoPE/NoPE/ALiBi/NAPE) and attention mechanisms (softmax/SSMax/entmax/ASEntmax), demonstrating consistent and sometimes dramatic improvements in length extrapolation (e.g., 1000x on associative recall, 8x on Reverse).
Good supplementary empirical verification of theoretical claims (representational collapse and gradient-path/over-squashing experiments) that corroborate the proofs, going beyond pure theory.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on small synthetic algorithmic tasks with very small models (2-10M parameters, up to 120M only for a scaling-fit sanity check); there is no evaluation on real downstream long-context NLP benchmarks (e.g., RULER, LongBench, real language modeling perplexity at long context), making it unclear whether the claimed long-context generalization benefits transfer to practical LLM settings.

Results are somewhat inconsistent across tasks: Sort fails beyond 4x for every method regardless of attention/positional-encoding choice, NAPE does not always help (e.g., some Flip-Flop and Local Count configurations), and SEntmax/ASSMax sometimes degrade sharply at specific lengths (e.g., MQMTAR SEntmax collapsing to near-zero at 8192+), suggesting fragility and sensitivity to task-specific tuning rather than a universal mechanism.

The paper reports 'the single best-performing model selected from experiments conducted with multiple random seeds (3) and various learning rates' rather than mean/variance across seeds, raising reproducibility and cherry-picking concerns, especially given how large some reported effects are.

Key hyperparameters (e.g., δ=1, α=1.5 default, specific ALiBi slopes, RoPE scaling factor of 16) appear to be manually tuned per task without systematic sensitivity analysis beyond a couple of ablation tables, limiting confidence in robustness.

The theoretical guarantees (bounded entropy, support size s ≪ n) rely on the attention support staying sparse; however, ASEntmax's learned scaling can push the distribution toward dense softmax-like regimes, so the practical sparsity level (and thus whether the proven guarantees actually hold) is not empirically verified/quantified in the trained models.

Missing comparisons with other established efficient/sparse long-context methods (e.g., Longformer, BigBird, sliding-window variants, or other recent length-generalization techniques) on the same synthetic benchmarks, limiting the positioning of the sparsity argument relative to simpler fixed-pattern sparse attention baselines.

strengths: Strong and rigorous theoretical contribution: the paper formally defines attention dispersion and proves that softmax exhibits complete dispersion while α-entmax can exhibit concentration resilience (bounded normalized entropy), directly linking sparsity to non-dispersion, representational preservation, and reduced gradient paths (over-squashing alleviation). Proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained in the appendix.

The theoretical analysis is paired with targeted empirical verification (e.g., representational collapse counterexample up to 128K tokens, gradient-path/gradient-norm experiments on a copying task), which strengthens the credibility of the claims beyond pure theory.

Introduces ASEntmax, a simple but well-motivated extension (head-specific, input-dependent power-law scaling with a γ exponent) that is shown empirically to be necessary via curve-fitting analysis on real trained models (Figure 3), not just synthetic argument.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation: multiple synthetic tasks (retrieval, memory, ordering) covering different generalization regimes, plus language modeling with short-context benchmarks, long-context perplexity, and RULER retrieval tasks, along with thorough ablations across positional encoding schemes (NoPE, ALiBi, RoPE, NAPE) and baselines (Top-K, SSMax, Adaptive Temperature, Stick-Breaking Attention).

Achieves striking extrapolation results (e.g., 1000x length generalization on MQMTAR, 8x context extrapolation with decreasing perplexity in language modeling), which are compelling evidence for the practical value of the approach.
Good engineering practicality: leverages existing efficient sparse attention kernels (AdaSplash) so the method does not require new hardware-level kernel engineering, aiding adoption.
Reproducibility statement and very detailed appendix (task descriptions, hyperparameters, additional ablations) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Language modeling experiments are conducted only at modest scale (120M and 420M parameters, 5-7B training tokens, 2048 training context), which leaves open whether the theoretical and empirical benefits persist at production scale (billions of parameters, much longer native contexts) as speculated in the conclusion.

The proposed method introduces several additional hyperparameters/design choices (α, δ, β, γ per head, NAPE's specific NoPE/ALiBi head split) that add complexity; the sensitivity to α or to the split ratio in NAPE is not deeply analyzed beyond default settings (α=1.5, δ=1).

Several results show α-entmax (without adaptive scaling) underperforming softmax or SSMax on specific tasks (e.g., Copy, PIQA), indicating the base sparsity assumption is not uniformly beneficial and that adaptive scaling is essential — this weakens the paper's central claim that sparsity alone is fundamentally superior, though the authors do reasonably note this and address it with ASEntmax.

Theoretical guarantees (e.g., Proposition 4 on over-squashing) rely on simplifying assumptions (independence of attention coefficients from values, constant approximation of layer norm) that may not hold in real trained networks, limiting the direct applicability of the formal bounds.

Comparisons are largely restricted to softmax-family variants (SSMax, Adaptive Temperature, Top-K, entmax); there is limited comparison against other prominent long-context approaches (e.g., state-space models, linear attention, or other structured/learned sparse attention methods beyond Stick-Breaking) that could contextualize the practical significance of the gains.

The NAPE positional encoding, which is used as the default configuration throughout main results, is explicitly stated as "not a contribution," yet it appears critical to most of the strong results, making it harder to disentangle how much of the improvement stems from ASEntmax itself versus the positional encoding interaction.

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical treatment: the paper provides formal definitions of attention dispersion, several propositions with full proofs (non-vanishing attention, entropy bounds, representational preservation, reduced gradient paths) that connect α-entmax's sparsity to three well-known long-context pathologies (dispersion, representational collapse, over-squashing).

Extensive empirical validation spanning many synthetic length-generalization tasks (MQMTAR, Max Retrieval, Copy, Reverse, Sort, Flip-Flop, 2Back, Local Count) as well as 420M-parameter language modeling with short-context benchmarks, long-context perplexity, and RULER retrieval tasks.

Careful, systematic study of the interaction between α-entmax and different positional encoding schemes (NoPE, ALiBi, RoPE, and the proposed NAPE hybrid), including theoretical propositions and empirical attention-centroid visualizations.

The proposed ASEntmax mechanism (head-specific, content- and length-dependent temperature scaling of α-entmax) is a reasonable and relatively simple extension that is compatible with existing fast sparse-attention kernels (AdaSplash), and the ablation on the γ exponent is a nice piece of evidence motivating the design.
Reasonably good reproducibility statement and large appendix with detailed experimental settings, extra tasks, and additional ablations (negative γ behavior, head-wise fits, etc.).
weaknesses: Scale of empirical validation is modest relative to the paper's claims about 'long-context generalization' for LLMs: the main language-modeling experiments use a 420M model trained on only 7B tokens with 2048-token context, and the head-scaling analysis uses a 120M model trained on 5B tokens. The conclusions about production-relevant long-context behavior are extrapolated from this small scale, and the authors themselves acknowledge this is only 'a foundation' for larger models, which weakens the significance of the practical claims.

NAPE (NoPE+ALiBi) is used as the default positional encoding in essentially all headline results, and the paper shows NAPE alone yields very large gains for every method (including softmax). Because ASEntmax's main results are reported with NAPE baked in, it is difficult to cleanly attribute the headline gains to ASEntmax itself versus the positional-encoding choice; the paper explicitly says NAPE is 'not a contribution' yet it appears to be doing much of the heavy lifting in the main tables.

Model selection methodology raises reproducibility/robustness concerns: 'we report results for the single best-performing model selected from experiments conducted with multiple random seeds (3) and various learning rates' with no variance/error bars reported anywhere, which could overstate the robustness of the reported gains, especially given synthetic-task accuracies that swing sharply (e.g., 0% to 95%) with small hyperparameter changes.

Mixed/inconsistent empirical story undercuts the 'ASEntmax is uniformly superior' narrative: SSMax outperforms ASEntmax on Copy and PIQA; plain Entmax underperforms Softmax on several tasks (Copy, Sort baseline) without adaptive scaling; Sort fails for all methods beyond 4x; results depend heavily on per-task tuning of α (e.g., α=16 needed for Max Retrieval but α=1.5 elsewhere), suggesting the practical method requires non-trivial task-specific tuning that is not clearly resolved by the 'adaptive' mechanism alone.

Several of the theoretical results (non-vanishing attention, zero probability for low-scoring tokens, bounded support entropy) are relatively direct consequences of already well-established properties of α-entmax/sparsemax (Peters et al. 2019; Martins et al. 2022) rather than fundamentally new insights; the contribution is largely in connecting known sparsity properties to the over-squashing/collapse framework of Barbero et al. (2024), which is more of a synthesis than a new theoretical mechanism.

No analysis of computational/wall-clock overhead or throughput trade-offs of α-entmax/AdaSplash vs. FlashAttention-based softmax at the scales tested, despite long-context efficiency being a central motivation for sparse attention research.

Baseline comparison, while including several recent related works (SSMax, Adaptive Temperature, Top-K, Stick-Breaking), omits broader comparison with other established long-context/efficient-attention approaches (e.g., sliding-window/local attention combined with global tokens, other recent entropy-aware scaling methods like InfoScale which is only discussed, not compared empirically) that would better contextualize the practical significance of the gains.

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution with rigorous proofs connecting α-entmax's sparsity to non-dispersion, representational preservation, and reduced gradient paths (over-squashing alleviation)
Extensive empirical validation across a diverse synthetic task suite (MQMTAR, Max Retrieval, Copy, Reverse, Sort, 2Back, Local Count, Flip-Flop) with careful positional-encoding ablations
Language modeling experiments at a non-trivial 420M-parameter scale with both short-context (6 QA/LM benchmarks) and long-context (perplexity, RULER NIAH) evaluation
Impressive and clearly demonstrated length extrapolation results (up to 1000x) substantially outperforming well-chosen baselines (SSMax, Adaptive Temperature, Top-K, fixed-alpha entmax)
Transparent reporting of failure cases (e.g., Sort, plain Entmax on Copy) with explanatory analysis and empirical verification (e.g., learned negative gamma values) rather than cherry-picked results
Practical and simple ASEntmax design compatible with existing fast sparse attention kernels, aiding adoptability
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, task descriptions, and reported code availability
weaknesses: Experiments capped at 420M parameters / 7B training tokens, leaving open whether benefits persist at production LLM scale

Headline length-generalization results are substantially entangled with the NAPE (NoPE+ALiBi) positional scheme introduced by the authors; results with pure RoPE are much weaker, complicating attribution of gains purely to entmax/ASEntmax
Some tasks show inconsistent or failing results across all methods (e.g., Sort beyond 4x), slightly undercutting the generality of the core claim

Several theoretical propositions (e.g., RoPE interaction analysis) rely on simplifying assumptions (small-angle approximations, value-independence of attention, constant LayerNorm) that may not hold tightly in practice
No comparison to other modern long-context approaches (e.g., state-space models, hybrid sliding-window/global-token attention), focusing mainly on softmax-variant baselines
Short-context performance preservation claim is only partially supported, as ASEntmax underperforms baselines on PIQA and WinoGrande, and several benchmarks are near-random for all methods
